title: Brent Crude Falls 16% to $98: Will Petrol Prices Drop in India?
snippet: Brent crude has recorded its sharpest weekly fall since 2020, trading near $98 per barrel. Find out whether the decline could make petrol and diesel cheaper in India.
content:
Brent Crude Falls 16% in a Week to $98; Will Petrol and Diesel Prices Drop in India?
Sandeep Patel
Brent crude has recorded its sharpest weekly fall since 2020, trading near $98 per barrel. Find out whether the decline could make petrol and diesel cheaper in India.
Global crude oil prices have fallen sharply, with Brent crude closing at around $98.32 per barrel on November 6 after losing nearly 16% over the week on a continuous-futures comparison. The decline followed a period of heightened prices amid the US-Iran conflict and concerns over possible disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
On Monday, November 9, Brent was trading around $98.35 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) was near $91.30. The latest movement came after US President Donald Trump indicated that fresh attacks on Iran were unlikely if negotiations made progress.
Brent Records Its Sharpest Weekly Fall Since 2020
Brent crude declined by approximately 16% during the week ended November 6, marking its steepest weekly percentage fall since the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
According to market data, Brent's continuous-futures price fell from around $117.64 on October 30 to $98.32 on November 6. The exact percentage varies depending on whether analysts compare continuous futures or specific monthly contracts.
In April 2020, crude prices had also witnessed an extraordinary weekly collapse as the pandemic severely affected global fuel demand. The current decline, however, is largely linked to changing expectations about the Middle East conflict and the outlook for oil supplies.
Hopes of US-Iran Peace Deal Push Oil Prices Lower
The possibility of a diplomatic settlement between Washington and Tehran has reduced concerns about prolonged supply disruptions.
The US midterm election results and Trump's latest comments have encouraged traders to expect a possible de-escalation. Markets are also factoring in signs of improving crude supplies from the Gulf region.
However, the situation remains uncertain. Reports of attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz have continued to raise concerns about the security of oil transportation. A renewed escalation could push prices higher again.
Three Important Oil Market Reports Due This Week
Investors will closely monitor upcoming reports from major energy organisations for fresh information on global demand, production and inventories.
-   Tuesday, November 10: US Energy Information Administration's Short-Term Energy Outlook is scheduled for release.
-   Wednesday, November 11: OPEC is scheduled to publish its monthly oil market report.
-   Friday, November 13: The International Energy Agency is scheduled to release its monthly Oil Market Report.
These reports could influence crude prices by providing updated forecasts on supply, consumption and market balances.
Why Crude Oil Prices Matter to India
India imports nearly 88% of its crude oil requirements, making the country highly exposed to changes in international oil prices. Government data put import dependence at approximately 88% during the financial years 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26.
When crude becomes expensive, Indian refiners and oil marketing companies face higher input costs. The country also spends more foreign exchange on imports, which can affect the trade balance, the rupee and inflation.
Higher fuel costs can eventually increase transportation and logistics expenses, putting pressure on prices of food, consumer goods and other essential products.
A sustained decline in crude prices, on the other hand, can reduce the country's import bill and ease cost pressures across the economy.
Will Petrol and Diesel Become Cheaper Immediately?
A fall in international crude prices does not automatically translate into an immediate reduction in retail fuel prices in India.
Petrol and diesel prices are influenced by several factors, including international product prices, the rupee-dollar exchange rate, refining and marketing costs, central excise duty, state VAT and dealer commissions. Oil marketing companies also consider their previous losses and margins while deciding retail prices.
As of November 9, petrol and diesel prices in major Indian cities remained largely unchanged despite the recent fall in crude prices.
Therefore, consumers should not assume that a 16% fall in Brent will lead to an equivalent reduction at fuel stations.
Oil Companies' Margins and Currency Rates Will Matter
The sustainability of the crude price decline will be crucial for Indian oil companies. If Brent remains around or below the $95–98 range for an extended period, refiners and fuel retailers could benefit from lower input costs.
However, a weaker rupee can offset some of the benefit because India pays for imported crude largely in US dollars. Refining margins, inventory costs and the prices of finished petrol and diesel in international markets will also influence the final impact.
Any reduction in retail fuel prices will ultimately depend on how much of the cost relief oil marketing companies are willing and able to pass on to consumers.
What Could Happen to Crude Prices Next?
The direction of the oil market will largely depend on developments in the US-Iran negotiations and the safety of shipping routes in the Gulf.
A diplomatic breakthrough could reduce the geopolitical premium further, while renewed attacks or restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz could reverse the recent decline.
For India, cheaper crude offers relief to the import bill and inflation outlook. But unless lower international prices remain sustained and domestic pricing conditions support a revision, petrol and diesel consumers may have to wait for relief.

title: IEA: Oil Supply Tops Demand for First Time Since Iran War
snippet: IEA says global oil supply hit 105.4 mb/d in October, topping demand, but Gulf exports 26% below pre-war and on-land stocks ...
content:
DHAHRAN — Global oil supply exceeded demand in October for the first time since the war in Iran began, the International Energy Agency said in its November Oil Market Report, published on November 13. World supply rose 2.3 million barrels a day in the month to 105.4 million b/d, but Gulf exports were still 26% below pre-war levels and stocks held on land fell to their lowest since at least 2016, the agency said.
The report describes a market that has loosened on paper but not in the tanks where refiners draw their crude. Most of October’s inventory build sat aboard ships rather than in storage, diesel remains the agency’s “overriding concern”, and on November 29 the 21 countries of OPEC+ meet to set their production framework for 2027 against those numbers.
The House of Saud Daily Briefing
Saudi Arabia's news in 3 minutes, every morning. Free. See today's issue
What the IEA Found in Its November Report
The agency’s central finding was a single line: the oil market is showing “tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” it said, according to Reuters. The war began in late February, when the United States and Israel struck Iran, and the disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has shaped every IEA report since.
The supply recovery behind the shift was fast. Global output has risen 5.3 million b/d since August, a rise the IEA called “extraordinary,” The National reported. The year-on-year shortfall in world supply narrowed to 2.9 million b/d in October, against an average loss of 8 million b/d between March and September.
The agency also rewrote its forecast for the rest of the year. Its estimate for fourth-quarter supply rose by 3.3 million b/d from the October report, according to Reuters and The National. Reuters calculated that supply in the quarter would average 105 million b/d, about 1.7 million b/d above forecast demand; Bloomberg put the gap closer to 2 million b/d, according to a summary of both reports by MLQ.ai.
Demand is moving the other way. The IEA forecast world consumption would fall 2.7 million b/d in 2026 to 102.3 million b/d, before recovering by 2 million b/d in 2027. On the supply side, it expects output to rise 6.6 million b/d next year to 108.1 million b/d, leaving a 2027 surplus of about 3.8 million b/d, according to Reuters via Business Recorder.

Why Are Stocks on Land Still Falling in a Surplus?
Because the surplus is at sea. Observed global inventories rose 52 million barrels in October, the first increase since June, but oil on water jumped 86 million barrels to its highest level since January, according to MLQ.ai’s account of the IEA report. Stocks on land kept falling.
The arithmetic of that split matters to refiners. A barrel loaded in the Gulf and still at sea counts as supply in the IEA’s balance but cannot be run through a refinery in Rotterdam or Ulsan. OECD stocks fell 47 million barrels in the month, and observed global inventories remain 462 million barrels below where they stood when the war began, the agency said.
Sultan Al Jaber, the chief executive of ADNOC, put the loss higher. Speaking at the ADIPEC conference in Abu Dhabi on November 2, he said the world had drawn nearly 1 billion barrels from inventories since the Hormuz disruption began, Khaleej Times reported. The two figures measure different things — the IEA counts only observed stocks.
Shipping costs explain part of why so much oil is afloat. Freight for very large crude carriers from the Gulf to China peaked at $36.97 a barrel on October 30 and was $35.60 a barrel a week later, according to a November 6 note from the analytics firm Kpler, which said price discovery remained thin because direct Hormuz loadings are low and privately fixed. Freight for Middle East crude bound for Asia stayed near record levels through October, according to MLQ.ai’s summary of the IEA report.
Gulf Exports Remain 26% Below Pre-War Levels
The recovery in Gulf supply is real but partial. Exports from Gulf producers excluding Oman reached 18.4 million b/d in October, still 26% below pre-war levels because of continuing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, The National reported, citing the IEA. Crude flows alone were 15 million b/d, or 82% of pre-war volumes, according to MLQ.ai’s summary of the report; refined products and LPG remained at about half of pre-war levels.
Independent estimates land in the same place. Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of FGE NexantECA, put Middle Eastern crude exports at roughly 80% to 85% of pre-war levels including pipeline volumes, and refined products at around 35% to 40%, The Edge reported on November 10. One month earlier, in its October report, the IEA had put September Gulf crude exports at 13.9 million b/d, according to Oil & Gas Journal.
The IEA’s warning on what could undo the recovery was direct: “attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery.” The days around the report’s release supplied examples. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and navy claimed a run of tankers hit mines in and around the strait between November 10 and November 15, including an LNG carrier on November 13, according to Reuters, Al Arabiya and Mehr News Agency; those are Iranian claims, and independent confirmation of each incident has been uneven (see earlier Guard claims of tanker attacks and the November 15 supertanker claim).
Tehran is also deciding who passes. Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency on November 3 that ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar were exempt from its restrictions. “Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” he said, according to Al Jazeera, adding that Tehran would collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships while Qatari vessels would pass free.
The exemptions map onto the buyers who were already taking most of the oil. Of the 10.23 million b/d of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, “about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India,” Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at Kpler, told Al Jazeera. Iran’s own supply outlook is moving in the opposite direction: the IEA cut its 2027 supply growth forecast by 1.1 million b/d, partly because of a downgrade for Iran, which is under a US blockade that has curbed its exports, Reuters reported. Tehran’s wider terms for the waterway are set out in its response to Washington on Hormuz.
Diesel Prices Stay Near $180 in Europe
Crude is loosening faster than the fuels made from it. The IEA described tightness in refined products as “the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers,” according to MLQ.ai. European diesel prices have fallen 11% since early October but remain near $180 a barrel, 77% above pre-war levels, and The National reported the agency’s description of diesel supply as one of “severe tightness,” with prices at record levels, especially in the United States.
The gap traces back to the Gulf’s refineries and export terminals. In its October report the IEA said Middle East refined product exports were 1.9 million b/d in September against a pre-war level of 4.7 million b/d, and that it expected diesel tightness to extend well into 2027, Oil & Gas Journal reported. Attacks on Russian energy infrastructure are also cutting Russia’s diesel exports, the agency said in November.
Governments have reached for their reserves. IEA member countries will release a further 71 million barrels of emergency stocks through February, including 15 million barrels of diesel, according to Reuters. In the United States, the average retail diesel price was $6.127 a gallon on November 9, down 17 cents on the week, according to the Energy Information Administration, as reported by FleetOwner.
Al Jaber gave the Abu Dhabi conference a sharper measure of the shortage. Diesel inventories in some markets had fallen to their lowest seasonal levels in 35 years, he said on November 2, according to Khaleej Times.
What Does a Loosening Market Mean for Saudi Arabia?
The kingdom is pumping close to its pre-war rate into a market whose price has come off its peak. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it produced 10.563 million b/d in October, up from 8.372 million b/d in September and the highest since February, when it reported 10.882 million b/d, Reuters reported on November 11. That is Riyadh’s own figure, submitted directly to OPEC, rather than one of the secondary-source estimates the organisation also publishes; the full breakdown is in OPEC’s November report.
Prices are falling as volumes rise. North Sea Dated crude dropped 32% from $136 a barrel on October 8 to about $93, according to MLQ.ai’s summary of the IEA data. Brent futures traded at $95.71 a barrel shortly after the report’s release on November 13, down 0.1%, Reuters reported, and The National recorded Brent at $96.16 later the same afternoon.
The fiscal pressure was already visible before the surplus arrived. The Saudi Ministry of Finance now projects a 2026 budget deficit of 245 billion riyals ($65 billion), or 4.9% of GDP, against the 165 billion riyals it budgeted, Tim Callen of the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington wrote on October 1. Callen said oil prices and export volumes, the main inputs to that forecast, were “clouded in uncertainty,” and described the ministry’s forecast for non-oil growth as one that “looks quite optimistic.”
Saudi export routes remain under pressure of their own. The East-West pipeline, which carries crude to the Red Sea and has around 7 million b/d of capacity according to Aramco, has been a target: the Houthis said on November 12 that they had attacked the pipeline and Yanbu, according to 24 News HD and an Oilprice.com report cited by MLQ.ai (see the Houthi claim on Yanbu).
What Will OPEC+ Decide on November 29?
The November 29 ministerial meeting is expected to settle output quotas for 2027, and analysts see it as the harder decision. “Today’s decision was the easy one,” Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad Energy, said on November 1, when seven core members held their December targets steady. “The much more important test comes at the November 29 ministerial meeting, when OPEC+ will decide its 2027 production framework,” he said, according to Reuters.
Leon described the group’s problem in three parts. “OPEC+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027,” he said. “The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return.”
The group’s own output is already close to where it was before the war. OPEC+ pumped 41.23 million b/d of crude in October, up about 2.04 million b/d from September and 97% of its pre-war February volume of 42.72 million b/d, according to Reuters calculations. It will be setting 2027 targets without the United Arab Emirates as an OPEC member: the UAE quit the organisation in May, Reuters reported.
Supply from outside the group adds to the pressure. The IEA expects output from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Guyana and Argentina to rise 1.6 million b/d in 2026, Reuters reported. The agency’s 2027 surplus estimate of about 3.8 million b/d is slightly lower than the 3.94 million b/d it forecast a month earlier, a reduction driven largely by the lower outlook for Iran.
The IEA balances assume Gulf barrels keep flowing at rising rates. They depend on the same strait where, in the week the report was published, Iranian forces were still claiming mine strikes on passing tankers.
Frequently Asked Questions
How did the IEA’s November view differ from its October report?
In its October 14 report the IEA said global oil markets were expected to remain in deficit through the end of 2026, and that “next year’s recovery remains contingent on sustained improvements in Hormuz flows,” according to Oil & Gas Journal. At that point it estimated observed stocks had ended September 509 million barrels below end-February levels.
Do other forecasters agree on the size of the surplus?
Estimates vary. Reuters calculated a fourth-quarter surplus of about 1.7 million b/d from the IEA’s figures and Bloomberg about 2 million b/d, while JPMorgan had forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million b/d for October alone, Reuters reported. The figures use different periods and methods, so they are not directly comparable.
Which fuels will drive demand growth in 2027?
The IEA expects LPG, ethane and naphtha, mostly petrochemical feedstocks, to account for about 80% of the projected 2 million b/d rise in 2027 demand, The National reported. Transport fuels see only a modest gain because high prices are “accelerating electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet,” the agency said.
How much has the war added to the cost of moving oil?
ADNOC’s Sultan Al Jaber said on November 2 that shipping and logistics now account for about 30% of the cost of a barrel, up from about 5% before the war, according to Khaleej Times. He called for more strategic storage, refined product inventories and refining capacity closer to consumers.

title: Gold Price – Today’s Chart – Historical Data – Outlook - The Bull
snippet: Gold price, chart, and outlook. Why gold goes beyond a metal, to inflation hedge, safe haven, and central‑bank ...
content:
Gold’s role in the global financial system extends well beyond its status as a precious metal. It functions simultaneously as a hedge against inflation and currency debasement, a safe-haven asset during geopolitical stress, a central bank reserve diversification tool, and a portfolio stabiliser with no counterparty risk. These overlapping roles explain why the metal commands attention across institutional trading desks, sovereign wealth funds, and retail portfolios alike.
Price Data, Historicals
Expand the Recent Daily Prices, or Download historical price day for a more detailed overview.
Gold Price Chart Today
The current pullback from highs reflects a classic short-term tension within gold markets. Because gold pays no interest or dividend, its opportunity cost rises when real bond yields increase. When inflation data comes in hot and the Federal Reserve signals it may keep rates elevated for longer, the relative attractiveness of yield-bearing assets like US Treasuries increases, drawing capital away from non-yielding gold. The October CPI print crystallised exactly this dynamic, and the market reaction was immediate.
Those same inflationary pressures that temporarily pushed gold lower by strengthening the hawkish rate narrative are, over a longer time horizon, among the most powerful structural drivers of gold demand. Persistent inflation erodes the purchasing power of fiat currencies, making hard assets more attractive. When inflation is accompanied by slowing economic growth in a stagflation scenario, the case for gold becomes even more compelling, as central banks face a difficult trade-off between fighting inflation and supporting growth.
Adding further structural support is the trajectory of US fiscal policy. The US national debt continues to expand at an accelerating pace, and concerns about long-term dollar debasement have become a central theme in institutional gold research. Broader geoeconomic fragmentation, including the potential for fresh global tariff adjustments and ongoing de-dollarisation trends among emerging market central banks, reinforces this narrative.
Price Forecasts: 2027 and Beyond
Despite trimming some near-term projections to account for the possibility of additional Fed rate hikes in the near term, analysts have largely maintained their bullish medium-term outlooks for gold.
J.P. Morgan carries the most aggressive base-case forecast among major banks, projecting gold at $6,300 per ounce by Q4 2027, driven by sovereign debasement hedging and expectations of a return to monetary easing. Goldman Sachs targets $5,400 by end-2027, acknowledging that near-term Fed hawkishness will slow momentum but arguing that structural central bank demand will ultimately prevail.
UBS forecasts a range of $5,000-$5,400, with the bank expecting structural buyers to establish a firm floor near $4,000 before a renewed rally driven by reserve diversification. RBC Capital projects a 2027 average price of $5,250, with a subsequent target of $5,500 for 2028.
Commerzbank and Deutsche Bank sit in the $5,150-$5,200 range, citing stagflation hedging as the primary driver. HSBC is the most conservative among major institutions, targeting $4,925-$5,025 and pointing to persistent dollar strength and hawkish Fed policy as constraints on upside.
At the more bullish end of the spectrum, Citi estimates a 30% probability that gold reaches $6,000 by end-2027, while Bank of America has outlined an extreme tail-risk bull scenario targeting $8,000 per ounce, a figure that would represent a doubling from current levels and would require a significant deterioration in US fiscal credibility or a major geopolitical shock.
Why Gold?
Gold trading has increased in retail portfolios dramatically over recent years, but beyond the trading element, there is a structural case for holding the metal. Perhaps the most significant development underpinning gold’s long-term bull case is the behaviour of central banks. According to World Gold Council data, central bank net purchases rose 42% year-over-year in Q3 2026, reaching 321 metric tons for the quarter. China’s official gold reserves increased by approximately 26 tonnes in October 2026 alone, a purchase made through the price pullback rather than despite it.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs and UBS have highlighted this “price-insensitive” official sector buying as a crucial structural support mechanism. Unlike speculative traders who may sell into weakness, central banks accumulating reserves as part of a long-term de-dollarisation strategy are unlikely to be deterred by short-term yield dynamics. This buying behaviour is widely credited with establishing a firm support floor in the $3,850-$4,000 range, limiting the depth of the current correction.
The motivation for central bank accumulation remains diversification away from US dollar-denominated assets reduces exposure to geopolitical risk, sanctions risk, and the long-term consequences of US fiscal expansion. For countries in Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Eastern Europe, gold represents a neutral reserve asset that carries no sovereign counterparty risk.
What To Watch
For traders tracking gold from here, several macroeconomic indicators will be decisive. Federal Reserve policy remains the most immediate variable, with any shift in the December 2026 meeting outcome; whether a hike, a hold, or dovish forward guidance, likely to have a direct and near-instantaneous impact on gold prices.
The US Dollar Index is also closely correlated with gold in the short term, where a reversal of the dollar’s recent strength would likely provide immediate relief for gold prices.
Longer-dated real Treasury yields, particularly the 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) yield, serve as the most direct measure of gold’s opportunity cost and deserve close monitoring. On the structural side, quarterly World Gold Council data on central bank purchases will be critical for assessing whether the pace of official sector accumulation is accelerating, decelerating, or holding steady. US fiscal data, including Congressional Budget Office deficit projections and debt ceiling negotiations, will also influence the debasement narrative that underpins much of the long-term bull case.

title: Gold, Silver Retreat From Peaks As Bullion Rally Loses Steam - BW Businessworld
snippet: Gold has fallen Rs 34,484 and silver Rs 1.30 lakh from MCX contract highs as profit-taking and US rate expectations weigh on ...
content:
Gold and silver remain sharply below their respective MCX contract highs, with silver down around Rs 1.30 lakh per kg and gold lower by more than Rs 34,000 per 10 grams as of the Monday close. The correction follows a reversal in international bullion markets, with profit-taking, US interest-rate expectations and movements in bond yields influencing investor sentiment.
The sell-off follows a strong rally earlier in the year, with precious metals facing pressure from changing monetary policy expectations and portfolio-wide selling. While gold continues to draw longer-term support from geopolitical uncertainty and central-bank diversification, silver faces additional exposure to changes in industrial demand. 
Silver Bears The Brunt Of The Correction
Silver has witnessed a steeper correction than gold, reflecting its dual role as an investment asset and an industrial metal. Unlike gold, silver's price is influenced by both investment demand and industrial consumption. The metal is used in electronics, solar energy, and other manufacturing segments, making its outlook sensitive to changes in industrial activity. Developments in solar manufacturing, including efforts to reduce silver consumption per panel and substitute other materials, are also relevant to its demand outlook.
Gold Falls More Than Rs 34,000 From High
Gold prices have corrected by more than Rs 34,000 per 10 grams from their 52-week MCX contract high. The December futures contract's high of Rs 1,77,590 compares with a closing price of Rs 1,43,106 on Monday, representing a decline of Rs 34,484.
The correction follows a strong rally earlier in the year, when geopolitical uncertainty and safe-haven demand supported bullion prices. Gold has also benefited from central-bank diversification of reserves, although shorter-term price movements remain sensitive to changes in monetary policy expectations. Since gold does not generate interest income, higher interest rates and rising bond yields can reduce its relative appeal compared with interest-bearing assets. Conversely, expectations of lower borrowing costs tend to support demand for the metal.
US Dollar And Federal Reserve Policy In Focus
International bullion prices have also been influenced by movements in the US dollar and Treasury yields. A stronger dollar makes gold and silver more expensive for buyers using other currencies, potentially weighing on demand. Investors are tracking US inflation data and Federal Reserve policy signals for indications of the direction of interest rates. Expectations of tighter monetary policy can weigh on precious metals, while lower interest rates generally improve the appeal of non-yielding assets.
In international markets on 10 November, spot gold fell 0.4 per cent to USD 4,124.42 per ounce as of 0618 GMT, while spot silver declined 0.3 per cent to USD 53.22 per ounce. The movements followed profit-booking after gold had gained more than 1 per cent in the previous session. US gold futures for December delivery, meanwhile, rose 0.5 per cent to USD 4,133 per ounce, highlighting the distinction between movements in spot and futures markets. Investors were awaiting US consumer price inflation data on November 10 and producer price data scheduled for November 13 for further indications of the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory.
What Lies Ahead For Precious Metals
The near-term direction of gold and silver will depend on incoming economic data, movements in the dollar and bond yields, and geopolitical developments. Investors will continue to assess the implications of US inflation readings for Federal Reserve policy and the attractiveness of non-yielding assets.
For Indian bullion prices, international gold and silver rates and movements in the rupee-dollar exchange rate will remain important factors. Domestic futures prices can diverge from international benchmarks because of currency fluctuations, import-related costs and local market conditions.
The MCX morning session was closed on 10 November on account of Diwali Balipratipada, with trading scheduled to resume in the evening session. Consequently, the domestic price comparisons in this report are based on 9 November closing prices.

Stock Market Live Updates
Synopsis
Sensex Today | Nifty 50 Live Updates: Indian benchmark indices trade higher on Monday, supported by increased FPI buying and hopes of a decline in oil prices. The gains came after Dalal Street snapped its winning streak on Friday.

title: Gold Price Outlook: Why Gold Is Holding Up Despite 5% US Yields
snippet: 3 days ago · Gold is holding near its summer lows at about $4,014/oz even with the 10-year Treasury yield at 4.988% and a December Fed hike fully priced, and the gold price outlook now hinges on physical demand from central banks and a possible debasement trade in 2027-28.
content:
Gold Price Outlook: Why Gold Is Holding Up Despite 5% US Yields
Key Takeaways
- Gold trades at about $4,014/oz, roughly flat against its summer lows, even though the 10-year yield hit 4.988% and a 25 basis point December Fed hike is fully priced.
- Gold remains about 26% below its 28 January record close of $5,419.83, but leveraged holders have been flushed out and unlevered buyers now set the floor.
- Central-bank demand reached 321 tonnes in Q3 2026, up 42% year on year, while ETF holdings hit a record 4,256 tonnes after 211 tonnes of inflows.
- Jewellery and retail demand are weakening, with global jewellery down 17% and bar and coin down 19% year on year, so the floor limits downside but does not drive prices higher.
- Institutional 2027 forecasts span $4,650 to about $6,300, and Deutsche Bank treats debasement as a conditional 2027-28 thesis that needs a trigger such as Fed easing or financial repression.
The 10-year US Treasury yield closed at 4.988% on 10 November, oil is trading above $85 a barrel, and markets have fully priced a Federal Reserve rate hike for December. On that backdrop, gold should be falling hard. Instead, it is roughly flat against its summer lows, and that gap is the most important signal in the current gold price outlook.
Many investors still assume gold must sink when yields climb, because a metal that pays no interest looks less attractive next to a bond that does. Spot gold was about $4,014/oz on 11 November 2026. That is well below January’s record close of $5,419.83, but it is holding a level the rates backdrop suggests it should have lost.
Daniel Ghali, head of metals research at Deutsche Bank, argues the support is physical and structural. He also argues that a different force could take over in 2027-28.
Here is what is holding gold up, what could still push it lower, and where the bullish and cautious camps actually split.
Why is gold holding near its summer lows despite 5% yields?
On screen, the numbers point one way. US inflation came in hotter than expected in October, and the market moved quickly to price tighter policy:
- October CPI: up 0.4% month on month, with core CPI up 0.3% against a 0.2% consensus (Reuters, 10 November)
- 10-year yield: 4.988%, up 12.55 basis points on the day (a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point)
- WTI crude: settled at $86.04 a barrel
- Fed pricing: a 25 basis point December hike fully priced
Gold dipped to about $4,030 after the inflation data, and then it stopped falling.
The fall from peak was real. Measured from the 28 January record close to the 11 November spot price, gold has dropped about 26%, after touching an intraday record of $5,594.82 on 29 January. Some interview coverage cited a much smaller year-to-date decline, but that figure does not reconcile with the reported prices. Ghali’s point is narrower: gold has gone sideways against its summer lows while yields surged.
His explanation is about who owns the metal. Leveraged investors, who borrow to hold gold and face margin calls when prices drop, were flushed out during the drawdown. The buyers left behind are unlevered holders such as central banks, sovereign institutions and physical investors, who do not have to sell when funding costs rise.
Deutsche Bank’s read on demand Ghali describes physical demand as “exceptionally strong,” estimating it is probably matching earlier records by weight and exceeding them in dollar value.
That turns the correction into a reset rather than a breakdown. If gold can hold while real yields (interest rates after inflation) surge, the marginal buyer has changed, and your old rule of thumb that rising yields mean falling gold is now a weaker guide than it used to be.
Analysts increasingly argue that real rates, rather than the headline size of each Fed move, determine how gold reacts, which is why a hike that merely matches inflation can leave the metal largely unmoved.
When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first
What is the physical demand floor made of?
If the buyers have changed, the next question is who they are. The World Gold Council (WGC) data points to three groups: central banks, exchange-traded funds and Chinese households.
Official and ETF buyers
Central banks are the clearest reason gold has stopped behaving like a simple mirror of bond yields. The WGC estimates official-sector demand reached 321 tonnes in Q3 2026, up 42% year on year, taking January to September buying to 675 tonnes.
Only 120 tonnes of that Q3 figure was publicly disclosed, so the total is a WGC estimate. Much official buying goes unreported. The People’s Bank of China has extended its buying streak to 20 consecutive months, with reported reserves of 2,346 tonnes.
The motives explain why this demand persists. Governments want to diversify reserves, reduce exposure to the US dollar and to assets that can be frozen by sanctions, and protect against fiscal risk. None of those reasons disappears when the 10-year yield moves from 4.5% to 5%.
Official buying is part of a wider reserve diversification trend, in which sovereign institutions treat bullion as a hedge against currency concentration and geopolitical risk rather than as a yield-seeking asset.
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which are listed funds that hold physical gold on investors’ behalf, added 211 tonnes in Q3, lifting holdings to a record 4,256 tonnes.
China and price-driven demand destruction
Gold imported into China rarely leaves, which steadily drains supply from global markets. High prices are hurting jewellery buying, but property and currency worries are keeping household investment demand intact.
Volumes tell a more mixed story than values do. January to September demand totalled 3,881 tonnes, almost level with the 3,884-tonne 2025 record, while its value hit a record $566 billion.
| Demand segment | Q3 2026 figure | Direction | What it signals | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Central banks (WGC estimate) | 321 tonnes | Up 42% y/y | Price-insensitive strategic buying | 
| ETF inflows | 211 tonnes | Holdings at record 4,256 tonnes | Investment demand returning | 
| Global jewellery | 313 tonnes | Down 17% y/y | High prices cutting consumer volumes | 
| Global bar and coin | 268 tonnes | Down 19% y/y | Retail buyers deferring purchases | 
| China jewellery | 66 tonnes | Down 22% y/y | Price-driven demand destruction | 
The floor is real, but it is made of price-insensitive buyers. That limits how far gold can fall. It does not, on its own, push prices higher.
Why could debasement become the bigger driver in 2027-28?
If the floor explains the present, Ghali’s fiscal argument is about what comes next. Debasement means a government eroding the real value of its currency and debts, usually through inflation. In his view, it was not a major driver of last year’s rally, but it could become one as US interest costs climb.
The arithmetic is stark. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) puts net interest outlays at about $1.028 trillion in FY2026.
Interest now outranks defence CBO projections place US net interest roughly $110 billion above defence spending of $918 billion, a point Ghali highlights as evidence of mounting fiscal strain.
Net Interest Outlays are projected to reach $1.028 Trillion in FY2026, overtaking the $918 Billion budget for Defence Spending.
Here is the tension. High rates support the dollar and hold gold back today. Yet every Fed hike raises the cost of refinancing government debt, which adds to borrowing needs and strain. Over time, that strengthens the case for inflationary responses or financial repression, which means policies that keep rates below inflation so debt shrinks in real terms.
The thesis has serious challengers:
- Money-supply analysts argue gold tracks liquidity more than debt headlines. Ghali himself notes US money supply growth is now more in line with the economy than over the past 5, 10 and 20 years.
- Real-yield analysts point out that positive inflation-adjusted yields make bonds attractive against a metal with no coupon.
- Dollar analysts warn that a stronger currency makes gold costlier for non-US buyers.
History backs the caution. Positive real rates interrupted the 1970s gold bull market, and in 2013 taper pricing sent gold sharply lower despite strong physical demand.
Treat debasement as a conditional 2027-28 thesis, not a present driver. It needs a trigger, such as the Fed easing or governments leaning on repression, before it moves the price.
How do 2027-28 forecasts compare, and what could break the case?
That conditional thesis shows up in the forecasts. Banks broadly agree on the drivers (official buying, diversification, investment demand and fiscal uncertainty), with jewellery barely featuring. They disagree sharply on how much those drivers can lift prices.
| Institution | Outlook | Key reasoning | 
|---|---|---|

| Goldman Sachs | $4,800 end-2027 (cut from $5,400) | Higher-for-longer rates restrain private demand | 
| Citi | About $5,000 over 6-12 months | Macro uncertainty, diversification | 
| Jefferies | $5,000 in 2027 | Inflation, debt, debasement, central banks | 
| UBS CIO | $5,400 by September 2027 | Central-bank buying, debt, geopolitics | 
| JPMorgan Global Research | About $6,300 by end-2027 | Investment demand, potential rate cuts | 
The camps sort themselves out. The Reuters survey and Goldman are moderately bullish, UBS and Jefferies structurally bullish, and JPMorgan very bullish. Goldman’s cut is the telling one: it still expects central banks to buy about 60 tonnes a month, but sees high rates suppressing private buyers until cuts arrive from late 2027 into early 2028.
Institutional forecasts for 2027 gold prices range from a $4,650 median in a Reuters survey up to ~$6,300 from JPMorgan Global Research.
The main risks to the floor are specific:
- Further Fed hikes: a 25 basis point December move is priced, and the probability of 50 basis points has risen above 10%
- A stronger dollar, which cuts overseas buying power
- Slower central-bank buying, with September disclosed purchases at 61 tonnes
- Disinflation without monetisation, which would remove the debasement trigger
A range of roughly $4,650 to $6,300 tells you the debate is about rates and timing, not whether the floor exists. Your exposure is still rate-sensitive, and position sizing should reflect that.
Markets often react more to Fed statement language than to the size of the move itself, so forward guidance on December and beyond may matter more for gold than the hike.
What the gold price outlook hinges on from here
Gold now has a sturdier floor than in past cycles, built by central banks, diversification and Chinese absorption. That floor has not removed volatility. Real yields, the dollar and price-sensitive jewellery and retail buyers can still drive large corrections, as the 26% fall from January’s record showed.
The question to carry into 2027 is which story markets choose to price: continued monetary restraint, or the fiscal cost of high rates on roughly $1 trillion of annual US net interest.
Three signals will show which way it is breaking:
- The Fed’s path, starting with the size of the December move
- Monthly central-bank purchases reported by the WGC
- ETF flows, the clearest gauge of whether private buyers are coming back
ETF totals can also hide a regional ETF flow divergence, with Asian and Western funds moving in opposite directions within the same weeks, so headline holdings are only a partial gauge of private demand.

Investors should conduct their own research and consult with financial professionals before making investment decisions. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Financial projections are subject to market conditions and various risk factors.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is debasement and why does it matter for gold?
Debasement is a government eroding the real value of its currency and debts, usually through inflation. Deutsche Bank's Daniel Ghali argues it could become a major gold driver in 2027-28 as US net interest costs, projected at about $1.028 trillion in FY2026, keep climbing.
Why is gold not falling when US Treasury yields are near 5%?
Leveraged holders were flushed out during the drawdown, leaving unlevered buyers such as central banks, sovereign institutions and physical investors who do not have to sell when funding costs rise. That shift in ownership weakens the old rule that rising yields mean falling gold.
How much gold are central banks buying in 2026?
The World Gold Council estimates official-sector demand reached 321 tonnes in Q3 2026, up 42% year on year, taking January to September buying to 675 tonnes. Only 120 tonnes of the Q3 figure was publicly disclosed, so the total is an estimate.
What are the main gold price forecasts for 2027?
Forecasts range from a $4,650 median in the Reuters analyst survey to about $6,300 from JPMorgan Global Research by end-2027. Goldman Sachs sits at $4,800 after cutting from $5,400, while UBS and Jefferies point to $5,400 and $5,000.
What should gold investors watch after the December Fed decision?
Three signals matter most: the Fed's path starting with the size of the December move, monthly central-bank purchases reported by the WGC, and ETF flows as the clearest gauge of private buyers returning. The risks to the floor include a stronger dollar and slower central-bank buying.

title: Gold Price Rebound: Central Bank Demand Drives 2026 Rally
snippet: Discover how central bank gold demand is reshaping global reserves and what institutional forecasts mean for investors.
content:
Gold Price Rebound: Central Bank Demand Drives 2026 Rally
The Structural Forces Reshaping Gold's Role in the Global Monetary System
For centuries, gold has functioned as the ultimate store of value during periods of monetary instability. But something fundamentally different is happening in the current cycle. The architecture of demand has shifted. Where previous gold bull markets were ignited by retail speculation, ETF inflows chasing inflation hedges, or momentum trading, the engine driving the gold price rebound on central bank demand today is sovereign-level reserve policy. Central banks are not buying gold because they expect short-term price appreciation. They are buying it because the international monetary system is undergoing a slow but unmistakable structural transformation.
Understanding this distinction is critical for any investor trying to make sense of gold's recent 20% correction from its January 2026 record high, the competing institutional price forecasts, and whether the metal's current levels near US$4,199 per ounce represent a temporary dislocation or the beginning of a more prolonged repricing. Furthermore, gold in the global monetary system has increasingly become the subject of serious debate among reserve managers and policymakers alike.
When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first
Why This Gold Cycle Is Structurally Different
Reserve Diversification Has Replaced Speculation as the Core Demand Driver
The 2025 bull run that lifted gold prices by 65% was remarkable for its breadth and velocity. However, what made it durable was not speculative momentum. It was the scale and consistency of official-sector accumulation running beneath the surface of the broader market narrative.
Central banks across emerging markets and developing economies have been systematically adding gold to their reserve portfolios, reducing concentration risk in US dollar-denominated assets. This is not a reactive trade. It is a deliberate, long-duration policy shift that is largely insensitive to the kind of short-term interest rate movements that typically punish non-yielding assets. In addition, central bank gold demand has proven remarkably consistent even during periods of macroeconomic turbulence.
The following table illustrates how different demand types respond to macroeconomic shifts, highlighting why central bank buying represents a uniquely stable price floor:
| Demand Type | Price Sensitivity | Primary Motivation | Typical Holding Period | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Central Bank Buying | Low | Reserve diversification, de-dollarisation | Long-term / permanent | 
| ETF Inflows | High | Inflation hedging, macro uncertainty | Medium-term | 
| Retail / Speculative | Very High | Short-term price momentum | Short-term | 
| Jewellery / Industrial | Moderate | Cultural, functional use | Cyclical | 
The De-Dollarisation Thesis Remains Intact Despite Surface Cooling
On the surface, commentary from some market participants suggests that the so-called debasement trade has lost momentum in 2026. However, a more granular reading of the data tells a different story. The structural catalysts that made dollar diversification a rational policy objective for dozens of central banks have not disappeared. They have simply been temporarily overshadowed by near-term USD strength and oil market volatility.
The de-dollarisation dynamic follows a distinct logic that operates across a much longer timeframe than quarterly market cycles. Consider the sequence of events that has accelerated reserve diversification:
- Sanctions risk awareness: The freezing of Russian sovereign assets in 2022 signalled to central banks globally that USD-denominated reserves carry geopolitical counterparty risk that had previously been underappreciated.
- US fiscal trajectory concerns: Persistent and growing US fiscal deficits raise long-term questions about dollar credibility and the real value of Treasury holdings.
- Multipolar reserve system emergence: Emerging market central banks are actively reducing single-currency concentration risk as a matter of institutional risk management.
- Gold's neutrality advantage: Physical gold carries no counterparty risk, cannot be frozen, sanctioned, or devalued by a foreign government's policy decision.
- Centuries of monetary precedent: Gold has preserved purchasing power across every major monetary regime change in recorded history.
Gold's Price Journey: From Record Highs to a 20% Correction
Understanding the Sell-Off and What the Data Reveals
Spot gold reached an all-time record high in January 2026, capping a multi-year surge that had seen the metal become one of the best-performing major assets globally. The subsequent correction of more than 20%, bringing prices to approximately US$4,199 per ounce by mid-June 2026, was driven by a convergence of macro headwinds rather than any deterioration in the fundamental demand picture.
| Period | Price Level / Change | Key Driver | 
|---|---|---|
| Full Year 2025 | +65% | Safe-haven demand, USD weakness, geopolitical risk | 
| January 2026 Peak | Record high (all-time) | Momentum, macro uncertainty | 
| Mid-June 2026 | ~US$4,199/oz | USD strength, oil shock, equity liquidation | 
| Correction Magnitude | Over 20% from peak | Rising yields, inflation expectations | 
A critical dynamic that often surprises investors is the liquidity paradox of gold. During periods of acute equity market stress, such as the oil shock-induced turbulence of early 2026, gold is frequently sold not because investors have lost confidence in it, but because it is one of the most liquid assets available to cover margin calls and equity losses.
This forced selling temporarily disconnects gold's price from its underlying demand fundamentals. Historically, such dislocations have preceded sharp recoveries once the selling pressure exhausts itself and structural buyers re-enter the market at more attractive levels. Consequently, gold safe-haven dynamics remain central to understanding why these dislocations are ultimately temporary.
Institutional Price Forecasts: What the Major Money Managers Are Projecting
A Broad Consensus Points Significantly Higher From Current Levels
Despite the correction, institutional forecasters have not materially revised their medium-term gold outlooks downward. The core thesis of sustained central bank accumulation and structural reserve diversification remains the foundation of bullish price projections. According to J.P. Morgan's commodities research, the medium-term outlook for gold continues to reflect constructive fundamentals driven by persistent official-sector demand.
| Institution | Price Target | Target Timeframe | Scale Indicator | 
|---|---|---|---|
| State Street Investment Management | US$4,750 to US$5,500/oz | End of 2026 | Approximately US$4.1 trillion AUM | 
| DWS Asset Management | US$5,400/oz | Mid-2027 | Major European asset manager | 
| Goldman Sachs | Above current market levels | 2026 outlook | Tier-1 global investment bank | 
| J.P. Morgan | Above current market levels | 2026 outlook | Tier-1 global investment bank | 
State Street Investment Management's base-case projection of US$4,750 to US$5,500 per ounce by year-end 2026 implies a recovery of at least 13% from mid-June 2026 price levels. German asset manager DWS extends its constructive view further out, targeting US$5,400 per ounce by mid-2027.
Analysts at William Blair Investment Management have noted that while the debasement trade has softened in the near term, its underlying catalysts remain firmly in place. The return of central banks to net buying in April 2026, following a brief period of net sales in March, was cited as evidence that the structural accumulation trend is intact.
It is important to note that these forecasts represent institutional base-case scenarios and carry inherent uncertainty. Investors should treat price projections as analytical frameworks rather than guaranteed outcomes, as macroeconomic conditions, geopolitical developments, and monetary policy shifts can materially alter trajectories.
Central Bank Demand in 2026: Looking Beyond the Headline Data
Why Reported Figures May Significantly Understate True Accumulation
One of the most important and least-discussed aspects of the central bank gold demand story is the gap between reported purchasing figures and estimated actual accumulation. Official reporting to bodies like the International Monetary Fund involves reporting lags and voluntary disclosure, meaning that headline monthly purchase data frequently understates the true scale of sovereign buying activity.
Alternative market-flow methodologies, which track physical gold movements through trade data, custodial changes, and derivatives positioning, have generated materially higher estimates of central bank accumulation than official figures suggest. Estimates based on these alternative-flow approaches placed net central bank purchases in Q1 2026 at approximately 244 tonnes, a figure substantially above what conventional reporting indicated.
Key data points that reinforce the structural demand narrative include:
- Central banks returned to net buying in April 2026 after March net sales, demonstrating the resilience of the underlying trend.
- World Gold Council data indicated approximately 17 to 19 tonnes of central bank purchases in April 2026 alone.
- A survey of central bank reserve managers found that roughly 95% of respondents anticipated increasing their gold holdings over the following 12 months.
- China's central bank was reported to have maintained consecutive monthly gold purchases for 19 straight months through May 2026.
Furthermore, central bank gold reserves data reveals the remarkable persistence of accumulation programmes even during periods of elevated gold prices. The persistence of China's buying programme is particularly significant. At scale, consistent monthly accumulation from the world's largest foreign exchange reserve holder represents a structural demand flow that absorbs meaningful quantities of annual mine supply.
The Macro Headwinds Working Against a Rapid Gold Recovery
Balancing the Bull Case Against Genuine Near-Term Risks
A credible investment thesis requires honest accounting of the forces working against gold as much as those supporting it. In the current environment, several powerful macro headwinds are limiting the pace of recovery.
| Factor | Direction | Impact on Gold | Magnitude | 
|---|---|---|---|
| USD Strengthening | Headwind | Reduces international purchasing demand | High | 
| Rising Bond Yields | Headwind | Increases opportunity cost of holding gold | High | 
| Oil Shock / Inflation | Headwind | Reduces real return appeal | Moderate to High | 
| AI Capital Expenditure Boom | Headwind | Diverts institutional capital from safe havens | Moderate | 
| Central Bank Accumulation | Tailwind | Structural price floor support | High | 
| Middle East Diplomatic Progress | Tailwind | Eases oil-driven inflation expectations | Moderate | 
| De-Dollarisation Trend | Tailwind | Long-term structural demand driver | High | 
| Equity Market Volatility | Tailwind | Flight-to-safety demand spikes | Variable | 
The AI capital expenditure boom deserves particular attention as a less commonly discussed headwind. The extraordinary scale of technology infrastructure investment being directed toward data centres, semiconductor manufacturing, and AI compute capacity is absorbing institutional capital that might otherwise flow toward defensive allocations like gold. When high-conviction growth narratives compete for the same pool of institutional capital as traditional safe-haven assets, gold's relative attractiveness can be temporarily compressed even when its fundamental demand thesis remains intact.
The Geopolitical Nuance: Why Peace Could Be a Mixed Signal for Gold
Progress toward diplomatic resolution of Middle East tensions presents a genuinely complex scenario for precious metal investors. The intuitive assumption is that reduced geopolitical risk should weaken gold's safe-haven premium. However, the secondary effects cut the other way. A reduction in Middle East tensions would ease supply pressures on crude oil, which would in turn reduce oil-driven inflation expectations, which reduces the relative appeal of yield-bearing alternatives to gold. The net effect on gold is therefore ambiguous and context-dependent rather than straightforwardly negative.
Frequently Asked Questions: Gold Price Rebound and Central Bank Demand
Why are central banks buying so much gold right now?
Central banks are accelerating gold purchases primarily to diversify foreign exchange reserves away from US dollar-denominated assets, reduce counterparty risk, and hedge against long-term currency debasement. The trend has been reinforced by geopolitical fragmentation and the precedent set by sovereign asset freezes in recent years.
What is the gold price forecast for the end of 2026?
Institutional forecasters including State Street Investment Management project gold reaching between US$4,750 and US$5,500 per ounce by end-2026, while DWS targets US$5,400 by mid-2027. These projections assume continued central bank accumulation and a moderation of oil-driven inflation pressures.
Does rising interest rates always push gold prices lower?
Not necessarily. While higher yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets like gold, central bank demand driven by reserve policy rather than yield-seeking can offset this pressure and maintain a structural price floor even in rising-rate environments. The current cycle is a practical demonstration of this dynamic.
What caused gold to fall more than 20% from its January 2026 peak?
The correction resulted from a combination of US dollar strengthening, rising crude oil prices fuelling inflation expectations, higher bond yields increasing the appeal of yield-bearing alternatives, and investor liquidations to cover equity losses during oil shock-related market turbulence.
How does de-dollarisation support gold prices over the long term?
As nations reduce reliance on US dollar reserves, motivated by sanctions risk, fiscal sustainability concerns, and multipolar geopolitics, gold becomes the preferred neutral reserve asset. This creates a persistent, policy-driven demand base that supports prices independently of speculative or retail investor sentiment.
Key Takeaways: Contextualising the Gold Price Rebound Thesis
Three Scenarios Investors Should Monitor Heading Into Late 2026
The recovery thesis for gold rests on several conditions holding simultaneously. Investors tracking the gold price rebound on central bank demand narrative should monitor the following scenario pathways. In addition, record gold ETF inflows observed in 2025 suggest that institutional appetite beyond central banks could further amplify any recovery from current levels.
- Base case (recovery to US$4,750 to US$5,500): Central bank accumulation continues at or above 2025 pace, USD strength moderates as US fiscal concerns resurface, and oil prices stabilise as diplomatic progress reduces supply risk premiums.
- Bull case (above US$5,500): A resumption of broad USD weakness, acceleration of de-dollarisation purchasing from additional sovereign buyers, and equity market volatility driving safe-haven inflows simultaneously.
- Bear case (extended consolidation): Persistently high US bond yields, continued AI-driven capital rotation away from defensives, and a surprise cooling of central bank purchasing activity reported in official data.
The structural argument for gold does not depend on any single catalyst materialising. Central bank buying is functioning as a price floor absorber rather than a speculative accelerant. Even in the bear case, the scale of sovereign accumulation limits how far prices can fall before institutional buyers return in size.
The gold market in 2026 is not behaving like a classic speculative cycle. It is reflecting the slow, methodical reordering of global reserve strategy by institutions that operate on timelines measured in decades rather than quarters. Furthermore, analysts at Crux Investor have highlighted that strong central bank demand alongside price weakness has created a notable valuation gap in gold equities, adding another dimension to the investment case. That distinction matters enormously for how investors should interpret price corrections, evaluate forecasts, and position within their broader portfolios.

Readers should conduct independent research and seek professional financial advice before making investment decisions. title: Gold Price Outlook 2026: Can Rate Cuts and Central-Bank Buying Push Gold Above $5,000?
snippet: Aug 12, 2026 · Gold set a record near $5,600 in January 2026, then fell more than 20% in its worst quarter since 2013, before rebounding to challenge $4,500 on August 11. Read our analysis of the switch from war-inflation fear to rate-cut expectations, the central-bank buying that rules out a collapse, what major desks now forecast, and the key risks that decide whether the rebound holds.
content:
Gold Price Overview 2026: From $5,600 Record High to August Rebound
Gold has been one of the most volatile major assets in 2026. After reaching a record near $5,600 in January, it fell more than 20% during the second quarter before rebounding sharply in August. The move reflects a major shift in what is driving the market: from safe-haven demand, to inflation and rate fears, and then back toward expectations for easier monetary policy.
- Gold hit a record before entering a deep correction: After peaking near $5,600 in January, gold fell roughly 22% to 24% through the second quarter, marking its weakest quarterly performance since 2013.
- Inflation fears replaced safe-haven demand: The Iran war pushed oil prices and inflation expectations higher, shifting attention toward a potentially more hawkish Federal Reserve and higher real interest rates, both of which weighed on gold.
- The August rebound changed the market narrative: As the inflation shock faded, gold moved back toward $4,500 on August 11, while silver approached $85, as markets began pricing rate cuts back in.
- The rebound still needs confirmation: Further upside depends largely on whether the Fed actually delivers rate cuts and whether central-bank gold purchases recover.
- Real interest rates remain the key driver: Both the second-quarter selloff and the August rebound can be traced back to changing expectations for real rates, making them the central variable for gold’s next move.
Read More: What Is BingX CFD and How to Trade CFD on BingX? A Beginner's Guide (2026)
Gold Market 2026 at a Glance
| Item | Detail | What It Signals | 
| January high | Record near $5,589 to $5,608, silver above $90 | Peak of the rate-cut-plus-safe-haven trade | 
| Q2 drawdown | Down about 22% to 24%, worst quarter since 2013 | War inflation temporarily overrode the bull case | 
| Early August | Consolidation at $4,000 to $4,100, near $4,090 on Aug 4 | Inflation shock fading at the margin | 
| August 11 rebound | Challenged $4,500, silver near $85 | Market repricing rate cuts back in | 
| Dominant logic | Shifting from war inflation to rate cuts plus central-bank buying | The rebound is one signal of that switch | 
January to June, 2026: From $5,600 Record High to 22%–24% Drawdown
Gold surged to a record near $5,600 in January, supported by safe-haven demand and expectations for lower interest rates. The trend reversed in Q2 as the Iran conflict pushed oil prices and inflation expectations higher, forcing markets to price a more hawkish Fed. Gold then fell roughly 22% to 24%, marking its worst quarter since 2013.
July to August, 2026: Stabilization Near $4,000 and Rebound Toward $4,500
Gold stabilized near $4,000 to $4,100 in early August before rebounding toward $4,500 on August 11. As the inflation shock faded, markets began shifting back toward rate-cut expectations and structural central-bank demand, restoring part of the bullish case that had driven gold earlier in the year.
Why Is Gold Price Rising in August 2026? 3 Key Drivers
Gold’s rebound was driven by three forces moving in the same direction: easing inflation pressure, renewed rate-cut expectations, and stronger central-bank demand.
- War-driven inflation pressure began to fade: Earlier in the year, higher oil prices lifted inflation expectations and pushed markets toward a higher-for-longer Fed outlook, weighing on gold through real interest rates. As that pressure eased, one of the main bearish forces weakened.
- Rate-cut expectations returned: Markets shifted back toward monetary easing, lowering expected real rates and reducing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold. This became the strongest short-term catalyst behind the rebound.
- Central-bank buying strengthened: Official-sector gold purchases recovered after a softer start to the year, adding a more structural source of demand beneath the price move.
The distinction between these drivers matters. Rate expectations can reverse quickly after a Fed meeting or inflation surprise, while central-bank demand tends to move more gradually. That leaves the rebound supported, but still dependent on whether expected rate cuts are ultimately delivered.
Gold Price Drivers 2026: How Rate Cuts, Central-Bank Buying, and the US Dollar Affect Gold
Gold’s outlook is increasingly shaped by three forces: Federal Reserve policy, central-bank demand, and the US dollar. The common link is real interest rates. When markets price in rate cuts, expected real yields fall and the opportunity cost of holding gold declines, while stronger official-sector demand can reinforce the move.
1. Federal Reserve Policy: The Strongest Short-Term Driver
Gold reacts more to the expected path of interest rates than to the current policy rate. The rebound toward $4,500 therefore reflects markets pricing a more accommodative Fed outlook back into gold.
That also makes the rally sensitive to incoming policy signals. Faster or deeper rate cuts would support lower real yields and gold demand, while a hawkish shift in Fed guidance could quickly weaken the strongest short-term bullish driver.
Read More: July 2026 Fed Rate Decision: What the Hawkish FOMC Means for Stocks, Gold, and Interest Rates
| Metric | Reading | What It Means | 
| Next-meeting cut odds | ~89.4% for 25 bps | Easing is now the base case | 
| Larger-cut bet | ~10.6% for 50 bps | A tail of more aggressive easing | 
| ETF demand per 25 bps cut | ~60 tonnes within 6 months | Goldman's modeled transmission to demand | 
| Three cuts in 2026 | ~180 tonnes of ETF demand | Scale of the potential tailwind | 
2. Central-Bank Buying: The Structural Demand Floor
Central-bank demand provides a longer-term source of support. World Gold Council data published on July 30 showed that official purchases rebounded in Q2 after a weaker start to the year. Poland added 51 tonnes during the quarter, while China added 33 tonnes, its strongest quarterly purchase since Q4 2023.
The pace is still below recent records. First-half purchases totaled 346 tonnes, the weakest first half since 2022, suggesting that high gold prices may be limiting how aggressively central banks buy. The longer-term trend nevertheless remains supportive, driven by reserve diversification and reduced dependence on the US dollar.
| Period | Net Central-Bank Purchases | Comparison | 
| 2026 Q1 | 57 tonnes | A sharp low that fed early "buying is collapsing" fears | 
| 2026 Q2 | 289 tonnes | Up more than 5x quarter over quarter, a Q2 record, up 62% year over year | 
| 2026 first half | ~346 tonnes | Still the lowest first half since 2022 | 
3. The US Dollar and Real Rates: Still Important, but No Longer the Whole Story
A stronger dollar and higher real yields traditionally pressure gold, while a weaker dollar and falling real yields tend to support it. That relationship remains important, but it has become less reliable when central-bank demand and sovereign-risk concerns are strong.
Gold’s strength alongside periods of dollar resilience shows why the dollar alone is no longer enough to explain the market. For the second half of 2026, the more useful framework is to track Fed rate expectations, real yields, the dollar, and central-bank purchases together rather than treating any single factor as the dominant signal.
Gold Forecast 2026: Major Bank Targets Range From $4,000 to $6,300
Wall Street remains broadly constructive on gold into year-end, even after several institutions trimmed forecasts during the summer. Most published targets still sit at or above the current $4,500 level, with year-end or Q4 forecasts ranging from roughly $4,000 to $6,300.
| Institution | 2026 / Year-End View | Outlook | 
| J.P. Morgan | Q4 target $6,300 | Bullish, though its 2026 average forecast was lowered | 
| Wells Fargo | $6,100–$6,300 | Bullish, with targets raised significantly | 
| Bank of America | $6,000 | Bullish | 
| RBC | $5,723 in 2026 | Constructive, with $6,500 projected for 2027 | 
| UBS | $5,500 | Moderately bullish | 
| Standard Chartered | Q4 average $4,650, retest of $5,000 | Cautiously constructive | 
| Reuters analyst survey | 2026 median $4,509 | Near current levels after the first downgrade in 11 quarters | 
| HSBC / StoneX | $4,560 / $4,000 | More cautious | 
- Most institutional forecasts still lean higher: The majority of major-bank targets remain above the current gold price, with the most bullish forecasts clustered around $6,000 to $6,300.
- Recent forecast cuts were mainly about magnitude: Several institutions lowered average-price estimates as Fed expectations turned more hawkish and ETF demand slowed, but most did not abandon the broader bullish gold thesis.
- The structural case remains intact: Central-bank buying, geopolitical risk, government debt, and currency-diversification demand continue to support longer-term gold forecasts even as near-term targets become more dispersed.
3 Risks That Could Push Gold Back Toward $4,000
Gold’s rebound has improved the outlook for the second half of 2026, but the bullish case still depends on rates, inflation, and investment demand moving in the right direction.
- A hawkish Fed pivot: If inflation stays elevated and the Federal Reserve delays or reduces expected rate cuts, real-rate expectations could move higher again and put renewed pressure on gold. That could bring the $4,000 to $3,800 area back into focus.
- Renewed war-driven inflation: A fresh escalation in the Middle East could push oil and inflation expectations higher, weakening the rate-cut narrative that helped drive the rebound. This remains one of the biggest two-way risks for gold.
- Weaker central-bank and ETF demand: Central-bank purchases already slowed sharply earlier in the year, and softer investment demand contributed to several institutional forecast cuts. If official buying and ETF inflows weaken at the same time, gold could lose an important source of support.
What Comes Next for Gold: $5,000 Upside vs. $3,800 Support
The August rebound did something the first-half drawdown could not: it moved the market's attention back from war inflation to the rate-cut path, and that switch alone justifies the repricing toward $4,500.
But the composition matters. The move rests on two forces, a rate-cut chain that depends on the Fed actually delivering and a structural central-bank floor that is durable but stepping down in total volume, and only one of them is under the Fed's control. The rate-cut driver can reverse in a single hawkish statement; the buying floor moves slowly and quarter by quarter. If cuts are delivered and official buying holds, the bullish case strengthens; if the Middle East flares or inflation forces a pivot, the rebound can unwind.
The question is now a matter of delivery rather than direction, and the answer arrives with upcoming CPI and PCE prints, the next FOMC meeting, and the World Gold Council's Q3 buying data. Until then, positioning built on the August rebound is positioning built on the assumption that the Fed cuts and central banks keep buying. On the charts, $5,000 is the psychological threshold above, and $4,000 to $3,800 is the strong support zone below.

title: Gold Is Forecast to Climb as Central Banks Buy the Precious Metal
snippet: Aug 28, 2026 · Demand for gold from central banks is a key structural factor underpinning the metal’s rally, according to Lina Thomas, senior commodities analyst in Goldman Sachs Research, and Daan Struyven, co-head of Global Commodities Research.
content:
Gold is projected to extend its recent gains in the second half of 2026, even as growing use of some derivatives tied to the metal could be making gold prices more volatile, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the precious metal will rise to $4,900 per troy ounce by the end of the year. Gold rallied 15% from its mid-July low to around $4,600 per troy ounce as of August 25.
The metal is expected to rise as central banks continue diversifying their reserves and markets scale back expectations for US rate hikes in 2026.
Demand for gold from central banks is a key structural factor underpinning the metal’s rally, according to Lina Thomas, senior commodities analyst in Goldman Sachs Research, and Daan Struyven, co-head of Global Commodities Research.
“We continue to see elevated central bank gold accumulation as a multi-year trend, as central banks diversify their reserves to hedge geopolitical and financial risks, consistent with recent survey evidence,” Thomas and Struyven write.
Central banks have been diversifying their holdings using gold, which is considered less likely to be frozen than reserves held in foreign currencies. They have been buying gold at an increased rate since 2022, when G7 countries responded to the invasion of Ukraine by freezing Russian central bank assets in Europe.
Goldman Sachs Research expects central banks to buy an average of 50 tonnes of gold per month in 2026, up from an average of 17 tonnes per month before 2022.
Central bank purchases accelerated to 100 tonnes per month in June 2026 (on a three-month seasonally adjusted basis) from 66 tonnes the previous month, according to Goldman Sachs Research’s nowcast of central bank activity. China’s central bank was the largest identifiable buyer in the market in June.
Interest rate expectations are another important factor supporting recent gold price increases. Demand from some investors is starting to recover from a slow first half of the year as markets scale back expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in 2026.
Historically, gold tends to struggle when interest rates rise, as higher rates reduce the appeal of gold relative to yielding assets like bonds.
“We expect the Fed-related headwind to abate further, as our economists expect a lower inflation trend to keep the Fed on hold this year,” Thomas and Struyven write.
The researchers also highlight a range of medium-term factors that could cause the gold price to exceed Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for 2026. “Gold’s share in private portfolios remains low, and recent geopolitical developments—including Iran and broader tensions—may accelerate diversification beyond central banks to private investors, including by weighing on perceptions of Western fiscal sustainability.”
Demand for gold call options is rising as investors turn to the instruments to hedge their portfolios against large-scale changes in government policies. This has the potential to amplify price swings in both directions, Thomas and Struyven explain.
As gold rises, it is approaching key strike levels for some call options, forcing options dealers that sold these calls to buy gold in order to hedge their short exposure to the metal, accelerating the rally.
On the other hand, declines in the gold price could prompt dealers to reverse those hedges by selling their gold holdings, driving prices even lower.
Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for gold to reach $4,900 per troy ounce by the end of 2026 does not incorporate elevated demand for hedges through gold derivatives. This could increase the likelihood that the gold price exceeds the forecast, but it also suggests “greater two-sided volatility” to the gold rally, Thomas and Struyven write.
